questions.problem:
Given that $x=3$ and $x=-2$ are solutions to the equation ${x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+7x-30=0,$ find the remaining solutions in the form $a\pm b\,\text{i},$ where $b$ is **non-negative** number.

$x=$
{{field-1}}
$\pm $
{{field-2}}$\text{i}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+7x-30.$ Since ${x}_{1}=3$ and ${x}_{2}=-2$ are roots of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem, 

$$
(x-3)(x+2)={x}^{2}-x-6
$$

is a factor of $f(x).$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-x-6$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,{x}^{2}-2x+5 \\ {x}^{2}-x-6 & \,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+7x-30\,\,} \\  & \,{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,-2{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}+7x-30 \\  & \,{\,-\,2{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+12x}_{―} \\  & \,5{x}^{2}-5x-30 \\  & \,{5{x}^{2}-5x-30}_{―} \\  & \,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-x-6)({x}^{2}-2x+5).$

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}-2x+5=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+5 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-2x+1)+5-1 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =-4 \\ x-1 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ x & =1\pm 2\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the remaining solutions to our original equation, apart from $x=3$ and $x=-2,$ are $x=1\pm 2\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Given that $x=-2-5\text{i}$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+18{x}^{2}-122x+377=0,$ find the remaining solutions in the form $a\pm b\,\text{i},$ where $b$ is **non-negative** number.

$x=-2\,+$
{{field-1}}$\text{i}\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}
$\pm $
{{field-3}}$\text{i}$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+18{x}^{2}-122x+377.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-2-5\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-2-5\text{i}}=-2+5\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(-2+5\text{i}))(x-(-2-5\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(-2+5\text{i}))(x-(-2-5\text{i})) & ={x}^{2}-(-2-5\text{i})x-(-2+5\text{i})x+(-2-5\text{i})(-2+5\text{i}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+4x+((-2)^{2}-(5\text{i})^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+4x+29.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+4x+29$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,{x}^{2}-6x+13 \\ {x}^{2}+4x+29 & \,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+18{x}^{2}-122x+377\,\,} \\  & \,{{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+29{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,-6{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}-122x \\  & \,\,\,{-6{x}^{3}-24{x}^{2}-174x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,13{x}^{2}+52x+377 \\  & \,\,\,{13{x}^{2}+52x+377}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+4x+29)({x}^{2}-6x+13).$

To find the other two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}-6x+13=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+13 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-6x+9)+13-9 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =-4 \\ x-3 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ x & =3\pm 2\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the remaining solutions to our original equation, apart from $x=-2-5\text{i},$ are
$x=-2+5\,\text{i}$
and
$x=3\pm 2\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Given that $x=4-\text{i}$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+26{x}^{2}-72x+153=0,$ find the remaining solutions in the form $a\pm b\,\text{i},$ where $b$ is **non-negative** number.

$x=4\,+$
{{field-1}}$\text{i}\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}
$\pm $
{{field-3}}$\text{i}$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+26{x}^{2}-72x+153.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=4-\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{4-\text{i}}=4+\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(4+\text{i}))(x-(4-\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(4+\text{i}))(x-(4-\text{i})) & ={x}^{2}-(4-\text{i})x-(4+\text{i})x+(4-\text{i})(4+\text{i}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+({4}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+17.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-8x+17$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,{x}^{2}+9 \\ {x}^{2}-8x+17 & \,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+26{x}^{2}-72x+153\,\,} \\  & \,{{x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+17{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,9{x}^{2}-72x+153 \\  & \,{9{x}^{2}-72x+153}_{―} \\  & \,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-8x+17)({x}^{2}+9).$

To find the other two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}+9=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =-9 \\ x & =\pm 3\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the remaining solutions to our original equation, apart from $x=4-\text{i},$ are
$x=4+1\,\text{i}$
and
$x=0\pm 3\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Given that $x=3-4\,\text{i}$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}+76x+100=0,$ find the remaining solutions.

$x=$
{{field-1}}
$+$
{{field-2}}$\text{i},$ 
 and $\,x=$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}+76x+100.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=3-4\,\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{3-4\,\text{i}}=3+4\,\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, $(x-(3-4\,\text{i}))(x-(3+4\,\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(3-4\,\text{i}))(x-(3+4\,\text{i})) & ={x}^{2}-(3+4\,\text{i})x-(3-4\,\text{i})x+(3-4\,\text{i})(3+4\,\text{i}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+({3}^{2}-(4\text{i})^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+25.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-6x+25$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,{x}^{2}+4x+4 \\ {x}^{2}-6x+25 & \,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}+76x+100\,\,} \\  & \,{{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3}+25{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,4{x}^{3}-20{x}^{2}+76x \\  & \,{\,\,4{x}^{3}-24{x}^{2}+100x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,4{x}^{2}-24x+100 \\  & \,\,\,{4{x}^{2}-24x+100}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-6x+25)({x}^{2}+4x+4).$

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}+4x+4=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+4 & =0 \\ (x+2)(x+2) & =0 \\ (x+2)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the remaining solutions to our original equation, apart from $x=3-4\,\text{i},$ are
$x=3+4\,\text{i}$
and
$x=-2.$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $x=2\textrm{i}$ is a solution to the quartic equation $x^4 + 13 x^2 + 36 = 0$, find all of the solutions.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x) = x^4 + 13 x^2 + 36.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and $x_1=2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overline{x_1}=\overline{2\textrm{i}}=-2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$\big(x-2\text{i}\big)\big(x-(-2\text{i})\big)$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2\text{i})(x-(-2\text{i})) & =(x-2\text{i})(x+2\text{i}) \\  & =({x}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $x^2+4$ using long division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{x}^{2}+9 \\  & {x}^{2}+4\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}+13{x}^{2}+36\,\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{4}+4{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,9{x}^{2}+36 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{9{x}^{2}+36}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x) = (x^2+4)(x^2+9).$

To find the other two roots, we solve $x^2+9 = 0{:}$
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =-9 \\ x & =\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 Therefore, the roots of our quartic equation are $x=\pm 2\textrm{i}, \, \pm 3 \textrm{i}.$
